findings.title: Denial cache key omits identity type, so renderer and anonymous share denials
findings.body: `userPermDenialCacheKey` is built from `checkReq.UserUID` (the raw subject ID), not the identity type. `anonymous:0` and `render:0` both yield UserUID `0` (the tests use exactly these subjects). If an anonymous check on dashboard X is denied, the key `<ns>.perm_0_dashboards:read_X_<folder>` is stored. A `render:0` check on the same dashboard within 30s then hits that entry in `Check` and is denied. The renderer holds a wildcard read grant, so image rendering can fail spuriously. Include the identity type in the key.

findings.title: Underscore-joined denial key is ambiguous and can deny the wrong resource
findings.body: The key joins userUID, action, name and parent with `_`, and these values can contain underscores. `(name="a_b", parent="c")` and `(name="a", parent="b_c")` both produce `..._a_b_c`. A cached denial for one resource then wrongly denies the other for up to 30s. The key also starts with the same `perm_<uid>_<action>` prefix as `userPermCacheKey`, which makes cross-key clashes possible if values contain underscores. Use an unambiguous separator or encoding, or a distinct prefix such as `perm_denied_`.

findings.title: Every non-allowed check not already in the denial cache hits the permission DB
findings.body: Cached permissions that do not allow the request now fall through to `getIdentityPermissions`. `getUserPermissions` no longer consults `permCache`, so it always runs the permission query, and the denial cache is keyed per (name, folder). A user or client probing many distinct resources the user cannot access triggers one full permission query per resource. Singleflight only dedups concurrent calls for the same user and action. The first denied check for each resource therefore costs a DB round trip, which amplifies load. Consider rate-limiting the refetch, for example a short per-user/action refresh cooldown, instead of re-querying on every miss.

findings.title: Requery path still uses a stale cached folder tree, then caches the resulting denial
findings.body: After a cache miss, permissions are re-fetched from the DB, but `checkPermission` → `checkInheritedPermissions` → `buildFolderTree` still reads the folder tree from `folderCache` (30s TTL). Suppose a user with inherited access via parent folder P creates subfolder C and a dashboard in C. If the cached tree predates C, `tree.Ancestors(C)` is empty, so the check returns denied. This PR then writes a 30s denial entry for it. The newly created nested folder or dashboard stays inaccessible for up to 30s, which is the scenario the PR is meant to fix. The folder tree should be refreshed on the requery path, or denials caused by a possibly stale tree should not be cached.

findings.title: Denial entries are never invalidated and can mask a permission granted shortly after
findings.body: A denial is cached for 30s with no invalidation. It is checked before the cached permissions and before the DB requery. If a check for a resource runs before its permission rows exist, or before a grant takes effect, the user is denied for the full TTL even though the DB now allows it. For example, a check may run between resource creation and permission assignment. That is the same "cannot fetch what I just created" symptom the PR targets. Consider a much shorter TTL for denials, or invalidation on resource creation or permission change.

findings.title: Tests do not cover writing the denial entry, and a dead cacheHit branch remains
findings.body: `TestService_CacheCheck` only checks that a pre-seeded denial entry is honored. No test verifies that a real denied `Check` writes `permDenialCache`, that a repeated denied check skips the DB (via `store.calls`), or that anonymous and renderer identities are handled. List fallback to the DB on a cache miss is untested. Separately, removing the "cached" case from `TestService_getUserPermissions` leaves the `cacheHit` field and its assertions as dead code, because no case sets `cacheHit: true`.
